title: Jobs and Skills Australia (National Skills Commissioner Repeal) Bill 2022
short_title: Jobs and Skills Australia (National Skills Commissioner Repeal) Bill 2022

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill is part of a package that would create a new advisory body called Jobs and Skills Australia and, in a separate companion bill, abolish the National Skills Commissioner.

The new agency would research and analyze workforce needs, consult with governments and industry, and advise the relevant ministers, with an interim director appointed by the minister to lead it initially.
The package aims to improve employment opportunities and strengthen the economy, and the government plans to introduce a further bill later to set the agency's permanent design.
changes: Establishing Jobs and Skills Australia as a statutory body within the employment department.
Repealing the National Skills Commissioner Act 2020.
Requiring Jobs and Skills Australia to consult with state and territory governments and key stakeholders.
Providing for an interim director to lead the agency and support a transition to a permanent model.
summary.affected: Individuals seeking employment, employers, unions, training providers, and state and territory governments would be affected by the new advisory body and the repeal of the commissioner role.

speeches.speaker: Brendan Patrick John O'Connor
speeches.brief: The Jobs and Skills Australia (National Skills Commissioner Repeal) Bill 2022 repeals the National Skills Commissioner Act 2020 to establish a more strategic, collaborative approach to workforce and skills planning, involving industry, employers, unions, governments, and training providers.

speeches.speaker: Ged Kearney
speeches.brief: The speaker argued for the Jobs and Skills Australia Bill 2022, establishing an independent agency to provide labour market advice through tripartism, and criticised the previous government for cutting $3 billion from VET and ignoring workers. Concrete commitments include 465,000 fee-free TAFE places, new energy apprenticeships, a full employment white paper, and a TAFE Technology Fund, with reference to Angela Merkel's praise for Australia's tripartite model.

speeches.speaker: Louise Miller-Frost
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Jobs and Skills Australia Bill to establish a statutory body providing independent advice on skills and workforce training, citing a 17% business shortage and 67% in higher skilled occupations, and announced measures including 180,000 fee-free TAFE places, 10,000 new energy apprenticeships, and a requirement for one in ten workers on major federal projects to be apprentices, trainees or cadets.

speeches.speaker: Shayne Kenneth Neumann
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Jobs and Skills Australia Bill 2022 and the National Skills Commissioner Repeal Bill 2022, arguing they deliver Labor's election commitment to establish a tripartite body with strategic independence, and criticised the former coalition government for cutting $3 billion from skills and training, resulting in 70,000 fewer apprenticeships and traineeships by May 2022.

speeches.speaker: Helen Haines
speeches.brief: The speaker backed the establishment of Jobs and Skills Australia but announced an amendment to add a dedicated function for rural, regional and remote skills and workforce advice, noting that regional organisations were not listed as key stakeholders. She cited labour shortages, housing barriers and ageing TAFE infrastructure in her electorate of Indi as key regional challenges.
